name: cheating
description: Perception that someone's words or actions reflect selfishness when they are expected to do the 'right' thing.

variations.name: someone else cheating
variations.description: When you perceive someone else cheating or lying, your reaction may range from laughter to anger to disgust. It depends on who's doing it, the importance of the rule, what they stand to gain, and how it affects you.

variations.name: relationship cheating
variations.description: Marital and sexual cheating creates outrage because it reflects poorly on one party and may create signficant costs.

variations.name: justified cheating
variations.description: If you're the one doing the cheating or lying, you'll likely have developed a narrative for why it's ok to break the rule.

variations.name: ignorance of the rules
variations.description: If the person legitimately cannot have been expected to know the rule, breaking it might been seen as less offensive.
examples: foreign traveller walking on the grass despite the sign
a very young child doing just about anything

variations.name: accidental cheating
variations.description: If you realize after the fact that you inadvertently broke a rule, there may be a feeling of guilt.

variations.name: self cheating
variations.description: Breaking a rule you set for yourself that no one else knows about or cares about.

variations.name: lying
variations.description: Speaking words that you know (or suspect) to be untrue but they're beneficial to you somehow.

variations.name: deception
variations.description: Acting or appearing in a way that hides your true nature in a way that's beneficial to you.

commentaries.quote: The more people rationalize cheating, the more it becomes a culture of dishonesty.
There's a reason behind every social rule. It's ok to formally renegotiate the nuance of a rule, but it's generally not cool to unilaterally consider yourself immune.
Ultimately, cheating is a decision that the individual is more important than the group.
Lying is easy because 'truth' is difficult. It may be worthwhile considering which you consider which patterns you tend to align with: individual preferences, social vibes, or existential context

Spreading misinformation is the same as polluting the mental environment despite the opportunity for social praise. If you wouldn't toss a piece of garbage out of your car window, you shouldn't fib, stretch the truth, spin, or gossip. On the otherhand, if you like whales dying from eating too much plastic, you should consider going into politics.

conditions: self perceives another agent breaking a social rule
judgment about the importance of the rule
judgment about how it affects you
judgment about whether the agent should know the rule
judgment about how the agent benefits from this action
